pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 36: Growing: pea (26 cm). Discovering: a door.*

The pea had grown twenty-six centimeters in three days. It was impressive, if you measured it, which I did, every hour, with my tape measure. But it had not flowered. It was just a long green rope of leaves that smelled like cut grass and nothing else. I was bored. Boredom is a dangerous thing when you are eleven and have a secret garden.

I followed a vine of honeysuckle behind the pear tree. It smelled sweet, heavy, and sticky, like the air before a storm. The hedge was thick, knotted with brown stems and sharp thorns that caught my denim jacket. I pushed through, tearing a small hole in the sleeve, but I did not care.

"Stop that," Gherkin said.

I froze. He was on his rock, looking exactly as bored as I felt.

"Mm. You found it," he said.

He said it quickly. That was what worried me. Gherkin never said anything quickly. He usually took four minutes to finish a sentence, often starting it in one breath and ending it in the next hour. But this time, there was no pause. No sigh. No "Mm." Just the words, rapid and crisp, like snapping dry twigs.

I looked past him. There, set into the heart of the hedge, was a door. It was small, painted a dull, fading green, with a brass handle shaped like a leaf. It looked like it had been there for a hundred years and was expecting me.
pages.image: A small, weathered green door with a brass leaf-shaped handle set into a thick, thorny hedge; Sana, thin with round glasses and a torn denim jacket, stands before it, looking surprised; Gherkin, a mossy tortoise, sits on a rock nearby.

pages.text:
I turned the handle. It did not squeak. It opened with a soft, heavy click, like a lock releasing a secret.

The air that hit my face was warm and smelled of pollen and old stone. It was late October outside, grey and damp, but inside the door was a room that had forgotten the season. Sunlight, thick and golden, slanted down through the leaves. Bees buzzed lazily in the air, fat with nectar.

The far wall was covered in roses. Not just a few, but hundreds. Red and white, climbing in spirals up the bricks. They were in full bloom, petals open and bright, defying the cold. The scent was so strong it made my head spin, like drinking too much milk.

At the foot of the wall, half-buried in the soil, stood a small stone. It was smooth and grey. On it was carved a single word: ADA.

I reached out to touch it, but my hand stopped in the air. The stone was cold, but the word felt warm. I looked at the roses, then at the stone, then at Gherkin, who was watching me with his unhurried, raisin-colored eyes.

"This is a lie," I whispered. "It’s October."

"Mm," Gherkin said. "Is it?"
pages.image: A lush, sunlit garden room with a brick wall covered in blooming red and white climbing roses; a small grey stone with no writing sits at the base; Sana, in a denim jacket, reaches out to touch the stone; bees float in the golden light.

pages.text:
Gherkin blinked. Once, then twice, before he began to speak. It took him four minutes to finish, which is a long time for a tortoise and an eternity for me.

"Ada was the first," he said, his voice low and slow. "She came to this garden on a Tuesday. It was raining. She met Mr. Osei. He was mopping the lift. She said one true thing."

"What did she say?" I asked.

"You do not need to know the words," Gherkin said. "You need to know the weight. Every rose on this wall is a true word. They bloom when someone in this garden tells the truth. When Ada died, they bloomed all at once. A burst. And they have not stopped since."

I stared at the flowers. "Why hasn’t Mr. Osei told anyone? He made this place. He has the keys."

Gherkin let out a long, dusty exhale, like leaves dragging across pavement. "Because he lost his nerve. He loved her. He kept the garden. But he forgot how to speak for it. He cannot bring himself to say it out loud. So he mops. And waits."

I looked at the door, then at the roses. The beauty felt heavy, like a coat I wasn’t wearing.
pages.image: Gherkin, the mossy tortoise, sits on a rock in a sunlit rose garden; Sana, with round glasses and a green pencil in her hair, listens intently, looking concerned; the background is filled with red and white roses and golden light.

pages.text:
"I want to tell him," I said, my voice coming out thinner than a sheet of pastry. I cleared my throat and tried again. "I want to tell him about the roses. About Ada. About the rules."

Gherkin looked at me. He moved his head to the left, slowly, like a camera panning.

"Not yet," he said.

I felt the heat rise in my cheeks, a sudden, uncomfortable flush. I was furious, the kind of hot, buzzing anger that makes you want to throw a shoe. I had never been so furious at a tortoise, or a person, or anything, really, except my mother when I wanted the last slice of bread.

"Why?" I demanded. "He is right there. He has been right there for years. We can tell him now. I have the tape measure. I can show him the growth. I can show him the rules. I can do it all in one go."

Gherkin blinked. "You cannot hurry a root, Sana. And you cannot hurry a person. People cannot be made to enter a garden. They have to open the gate themselves. If you push, they close the door. If you wait, they might walk in. Even if it takes a year."

I looked at the stone. ADA. I wanted to shake the whole hedge, to rattle the bricks until they fell down and revealed the secret.
pages.image: Sana, thin and angry, stands with hands on hips in front of Gherkin, who sits calmly on a rock; the background is a blurred garden with roses; Sana's face shows frustration and determination.

pages.text:
I walked out of the garden with my shoulders hunched and my fists tight. The air outside was cold again. The grey sky pressed down on the concrete blocks, making the whole estate feel small and trapped.

I climbed the stairs to the loading bay, my legs feeling heavy and leaden. I had to tell him. I had to say it. I was about to burst.

Mr. Osei was at the top of the stairs, holding a bucket. He looked tired. Not sleepy-tired, but the kind of tired that sits in your bones, like a stone you can’t shake out. He was mopping the same six square meters of floor.

"Mr. Osei," I said. My voice cracked.

He looked up. He nodded.

"I wanted to tell you something," I started. "About the garden. About Ada. About the roses. I know you know. I know you made it. I know you—"

"Good evening, Sana," he said.

He did not look at me. He looked at the floor. He squeezed the mop. Water dripped onto the concrete.

I stood there. I could see the words in my mouth, bubbling up, ready to spill. But I saw the way he held the mop, the way his shoulders were slumped. I saw that if I pushed, he would close the door.

"Good evening," I said.

It felt like the biggest thing I had ever held back. It hurt. It felt like swallowing a stone. But I kept my mouth shut.
pages.image: Mr. Osei, very tall with a grey moustache and blue overalls, mops a concrete floor with a mop and bucket; Sana, in a denim jacket, stands nearby, looking hesitant and serious; the lighting is dim and grey.
